rationale: The student says "b is tied to a" and that when "a becomes 7, b becomes 7 too," showing they believe assignment keeps two variables linked after the assignment.

The student says "other and nums are connected after other = nums, so whatever other gets, nums gets as well," expecting nums to change when other is reassigned — the classic linked-assignment belief.

The student writes "x = y means x passes its value over to y, so y becomes 10 and x stays 10," reading the assignment left-to-right so the left name gives its value to the right one. No function-tier or copy/linking ideas appear.
The student says "b = a gives b's 3 to a," treating assignment as copying from the left variable to the right variable. This is the reversed assignment misconception.

The student states "b = a makes b its own copy of the list, so appending to b does not affect a," which is the classic independent-copy belief for list assignment, predicting [1, 2] instead of [1, 2, 3].

The student says the function receives "a copy of data called items" and that appending to that copy leaves the original `data` empty, which is the copy-on-assign misconception for passing a list to a function.
The student says "f prints 3, and that's what it gives back, so y is 3," treating the printed output as the function's return value. This is exactly the print/return conflation in F1_RETURN_IS_PRINT.
The student predicts 8 appears in the output because "double(4) returns 8, and returning shows the number on the screen," conflating return with printing.
The student says "x is passed into bump as n, and n goes up by one, which means x goes up by one," i.e. reassigning the parameter n inside the function is believed to change the caller's variable x.
The student says "triple changes n to 6, and since n is x, x is 6 now too," showing the belief that reassigning the parameter n inside the function also changes the caller's variable x.

The student says "First the program hits greet, which prints hi," expecting the body of a function that is only defined (never called) to execute at the point of the def, before the later print("start").
The student says "Python reads top to bottom, so the print inside show happens first," expecting the body of show to execute when the def is reached, before print("B"), and then again at the call.
The student says that after calling make(), secret is still 42 and can be printed, treating the function-local variable as existing after the call ends.
The student says `value` is “still 3 from inside the function” after `setup()` returns, treating the function-local variable as existing in the caller’s scope.

The student says "The function returns n but keeps going to the next line and prints after," expecting the print after the return to execute. This is exactly the belief that execution continues past `return`.

The student acknowledges `return "pos"` is hit for x=5 but says "the last line also runs and returns non-pos, which replaces it," treating execution as continuing past the first return and letting a later return override it.

The student correctly treats n as a local name in bump's frame, says `n = n + 1` only rebinds n to 6, and that x outside still refers to 5 — correct notional-machine reasoning with no catalog misconceptions.

The student correctly distinguishes printing from returning: "f prints 3 but has no return, so it gives back None. y is None." This matches correct notional-machine reasoning, and the predicted output 3 | None is correct.

The student says "a and b are two names for the same list, so appending through b shows up when you print a," which is correct aliasing reasoning (no copy on assignment) and matches the correct output [1, 2, 3].

The student correctly states "secret only exists while make is running" and that it is "gone" once the call returns, showing an accurate understanding that the local frame disappears at the end of the call. No catalog misconception is present.

The student states "def just defines greet, it never gets called, so only start shows," correctly separating definition from execution and predicting only "start" prints. This is correct notional-machine reasoning.

The student predicted `6 6`, meaning they expect `x` to become 6 after `triple(x)` reassigns `n`. Although they say they are unsure, this prediction matches the typical F2 answer and nothing in their explanation contradicts it.

The student says `value` is still available after `setup()` returns and prints `4 3`, showing they think the local variable outlives the call. They also say “returning also shows the value,” conflating `return` with displaying output.
The student correctly predicted [1] and only said that append adds a 1, which is correct and does not reveal any listed misconception.
